name: Jesus Christ
summary: Jesus of Nazareth, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem in the days of Herod the Great, grew up in Nazareth as the son (as was supposed) of Joseph the carpenter. After his baptism by John in the Jordan he proclaimed the Kingdom of God in Galilee and Judea, called the Twelve, healed the sick, forgave sins, raised the dead and revealed the Father. At the Last Supper he instituted the Eucharist; he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, died and was buried, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven, promising and sending the Holy Spirit upon his Church.
catholic: The Church confesses Jesus Christ as one divine Person in two natures, true God and true man: 'consubstantial with the Father' (Nicaea, 325) and consubstantial with us, his natures united without confusion, change, division or separation (Chalcedon, 451; CCC 464-469). In the Incarnation the eternal Word took flesh of the Virgin Mary by the power of the Holy Spirit (Jn 1:14; CCC 461-463). His Passion, death, Resurrection and Ascension - the Paschal Mystery - accomplish our redemption and are made present in the liturgy, above all in the Eucharist he instituted at the Last Supper, 'the source and summit of the Christian life' (CCC 1324). He founded his Church on the apostles, with Peter as the rock (Mt 16:18), and remains present to it in word and sacrament until he comes again. Scripture presents him as the New Adam, the Son of David and heir of the promises to Abraham, the new Moses, one greater than Jonah and Solomon, and the fulfilment of the Law and the Prophets (Mt 5:17; Lk 24:27).
know: True God and true man: one divine Person in two natures (Council of Chalcedon, 451).
'Jesus' means 'God saves'; 'Christ' (Messiah) means 'Anointed One' (CCC 430, 436).
Born of the Virgin Mary; Joseph was his legal and foster father, through whom he is 'son of David' (Mt 1:16-25).
Instituted the Eucharist at the Last Supper: 'This is my body ... this is my blood' (Mt 26:26-28).
Crucified under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come again in glory (Apostles' and Nicene Creeds).
feast: December 25 (Christmas); Easter Sunday (movable); also the Epiphany, the Presentation (February 2), the Transfiguration (August 6), Corpus Christi, the Sacred Heart and Christ the King

name: David
summary: David, youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, was a shepherd anointed by Samuel, who killed Goliath, served and fled from Saul, and became king first of Judah at Hebron and then of all Israel. He captured Jerusalem, brought the Ark there with dancing and joy, and received God's covenant promise of an everlasting dynasty (2 Sam 7). He sinned gravely with Bathsheba and against Uriah, repented when Nathan confronted him, and suffered rebellion within his own house, especially Absalom's. He reigned forty years and prepared for the Temple his son Solomon would build.
catholic: David is a principal type of Christ: the shepherd-king born in Bethlehem, anointed with the Spirit, rejected before being enthroned. God's covenant through Nathan - 'your throne shall be established for ever' (2 Sam 7:16) - is fulfilled when Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son 'the throne of his father David' (Lk 1:32-33); 'Son of David' is the messianic title the crowds give Jesus (CCC 439). The Catechism calls David 'par excellence the king after God's own heart', a shepherd who prays for his people, whose submission to God's will, praise and repentance are a model of prayer (CCC 2579); Psalm 51, the Miserere, is the Church's great penitential psalm. His dancing before the Ark is echoed in the Visitation, when the unborn John leaps before Mary, the new Ark (CCC 2676). The Roman Martyrology commemorates holy King David on December 29.
know: Youngest son of Jesse; a shepherd of Bethlehem
Anointed by Samuel; killed Goliath
Made Jerusalem his capital and brought the Ark there
Received the Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7)
Sinned with Bathsheba and repented (Ps 51)
Jesus is hailed as 'Son of David'

name: Moses
summary: Levite born in Egypt under Pharaoh's death-decree, drawn from the Nile and raised by Pharaoh's daughter. After killing an Egyptian he fled to Midian, married Zipporah, and was called by God from the burning bush, where the divine name was revealed. He led Israel out of Egypt through the Red Sea, received the Law at Sinai, interceded for the people after the golden calf, and led them forty years in the wilderness; he died on Mount Nebo in sight of the promised land.
catholic: The Church sees Moses as the great type of Christ: the deliverer spared from a king's massacre, the mediator of the covenant, and the prophet who foretold 'a prophet like me' (Deut 18:15; Acts 3:22). The Law came through Moses, grace and truth through Jesus Christ (Jn 1:17); Moses gave manna, but the Father gives the true bread from heaven (Jn 6:32), and the bronze serpent he lifted up prefigures the Cross (Jn 3:14). The Catechism presents the burning bush and the revelation of the divine name (CCC 205-209) and Moses as the model of intercessory prayer (CCC 2574-2577). He appears with Elijah at the Transfiguration, and the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on September 4.
know: Name explained as 'drawn out of the water' (Exo 2:10).
Received God's name 'I AM WHO I AM' at the burning bush (Exo 3:14).
Led the Exodus and received the Ten Commandments at Sinai.
Called the most humble man on earth, speaking with God 'mouth to mouth' (Num 12:3-8).
Died on Mount Nebo; 'no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses' (Deut 34:10).

name: Jacob
summary: The younger twin of Isaac and Rebekah, who bought Esau's birthright and, with his mother's help, received Isaac's blessing. Fleeing to Laban, he dreamed at Bethel of a ladder reaching to heaven and received God's promise. He served Laban twenty years, married Leah and Rachel, and fathered twelve sons and a daughter. Returning, he wrestled with a mysterious man at Peniel and was renamed Israel; he went down to Egypt in old age, blessed his sons, and died there at 147.
catholic: Jesus applies Jacob's ladder to himself: 'you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (Jn 1:51), making Christ the true meeting-place of heaven and earth. The Catechism says the Church's tradition has retained Jacob's night-long wrestling as a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and the triumph of perseverance (CCC 2573). His words at Bethel, 'This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven' (Gen 28:17), are used in the liturgy for the dedication of a church. From his twelve sons come the twelve tribes, which the Church sees fulfilled in the twelve apostles and the new Israel.
know: Took Esau's birthright and blessing (Gen 25:29-34; 27)
Dreamed of the ladder at Bethel (Gen 28:10-22)
Married Leah and Rachel; father of the twelve tribes
Wrestled with God and was renamed Israel (Gen 32:22-32)
Jesus is the true 'Jacob's ladder' (Jn 1:51)

name: Aaron
summary: Elder brother of Moses, appointed by God as his spokesman before Pharaoh. He was anointed the first high priest of Israel, and his sons were made priests in perpetuity. He made the golden calf at the people's demand, joined Miriam in murmuring against Moses, and his rod alone budded when the tribes' rods were tested; he died on Mount Hor and his vestments passed to Eleazar.
catholic: The Church sees in Aaron's priesthood a prefiguration of the priesthood of the New Covenant. The Catechism teaches that the liturgy recognizes in the priesthood of Aaron and the service of the Levites a prefiguring of the ordained ministry, which is fulfilled in Christ, the one high priest (CCC 1539-1541; Heb 5:1-10). Hebrews contrasts Christ, a priest 'after the order of Melchizedek', with the Aaronic priests. Aaron's priestly blessing (Num 6:22-27) is the first reading on January 1, the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, and his rod that blossomed without root has been read in tradition as a figure of the Virgin's fruitfulness. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on July 1.
know: Moses' older brother and spokesman (Exo 4:14-16; 7:1).
Consecrated first high priest (Lev 8).
Made the golden calf (Exo 32).
His rod budded, blossomed and bore almonds (Num 17:8).
Died on Mount Hor at 123 (Num 33:39).

name: Saul
summary: Saul son of Kish, a tall young Benjaminite, was anointed by Samuel as Israel's first king and began well, rescuing Jabesh-gilead. But he offered sacrifice without waiting for Samuel and spared Agag and the spoil of Amalek, so the LORD rejected him as king. Tormented by an evil spirit and jealousy of David, he hunted David for years, consulted a medium at Endor, and died with three sons on Mount Gilboa.
catholic: Saul shows that anointing is a gift that requires obedience: 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Sam 15:22). As the first anointed king he stands at the start of the line of the 'messiah', the Anointed One, fulfilled in Christ (CCC 436). Fathers such as Augustine contrast proud Saul with humble David, and Saul of Tarsus - named after him and of the same tribe - recalls him in his sermon at Antioch (Acts 13:21). David's refusal to harm 'the LORD's anointed' is read on the 7th Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C) as a model of love of enemies.
know: Anointed by Samuel at Ramah
Rejected for disobedience over Amalek
Pursued David out of jealousy
Consulted the medium of Endor
Died by his own sword on Mount Gilboa

name: Abraham
summary: Called by God to leave his country and kindred for the land God would show him, Abram obeyed and received the promise that he would become a great nation and that all families of the earth would be blessed in him. God made a covenant with him, renamed him Abraham ('father of a multitude'), and in old age gave him Isaac by Sarah. When God tested him by commanding him to offer Isaac on Mount Moriah, he obeyed and God provided a ram instead; he died at 175 and was buried at Machpelah.
catholic: The Church honours Abraham as 'our father in faith', as the Roman Canon calls him, and the Catechism presents him as the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144-146) and of believing prayer (CCC 2570-2572). God's call to him begins the gathering of the People of God (CCC 59-60, 762), and his willingness to offer Isaac conforms him to the Father 'who did not spare his own Son' (CCC 2572; Rom 8:32). St Paul makes him the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile, justified by faith (Rom 4; Gal 3). Eastern tradition and Rublev's famous icon read the three visitors at Mamre (Gen 18) as a foreshadowing of the Trinity; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 9 October.
know: Called from Ur/Haran to the promised land (Gen 12:1-4)
'He believed in the LORD, who credited it to him for righteousness' (Gen 15:6)
Renamed from Abram to Abraham; circumcision as covenant sign (Gen 17)
Offered Isaac on Moriah; God provided the ram (Gen 22)
Called 'our father in faith' in the Roman Canon; feast 9 October

name: Solomon
summary: Solomon, son of David and Bathsheba (named Jedidiah, 'beloved of the LORD'), was anointed king through Nathan, Zadok and Bathsheba. At Gibeon he asked God for a listening heart to judge the people and received wisdom, riches and honour; his judgement between two mothers became proverbial. He built and dedicated the Temple in Jerusalem, where God's glory filled the house, and his fame drew the Queen of Sheba. But his many foreign wives turned his heart to other gods, and after his death the kingdom split.
catholic: Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the Temple is presented in the Catechism as a model of prayer: the Temple, the house of prayer David wanted to build, is the work of his son (CCC 2580). As son of David who builds God's house he fulfils 2 Sam 7:13 only in part; Jesus is the true Son of David and 'something greater than Solomon' (Mt 12:42) whose risen Body is the Temple (Jn 2:19-21). His prayer for wisdom (1 Kgs 3; Wis 9) is read on the 17th Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year A), and the wisdom books - Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs and Wisdom - are traditionally associated with him. His fall through idolatry is a warning that wisdom must be matched by fidelity.
know: Son of David and Bathsheba; also named Jedidiah
Asked God for wisdom at Gibeon
Built and dedicated the First Temple
Visited by the Queen of Sheba
Turned to idols in old age; the kingdom split after him

name: Joshua
role: Leader of Israel, successor of Moses
summary: Son of Nun of Ephraim, originally named Hoshea; Moses renamed him Joshua. He was Moses' assistant, fought Amalek at Rephidim, stayed at the Tent of Meeting, and with Caleb gave the faithful report about Canaan. Commissioned as Moses' successor, he led Israel across the Jordan, took Jericho and much of the land, divided it among the tribes, and before his death renewed the covenant at Shechem: 'As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.'
catholic: Joshua bears the same name as Jesus (Hebrew Yehoshua, 'the LORD saves'; Greek Iesous), and the Fathers, beginning with St. Justin Martyr, saw in him a vivid type of Christ: not Moses the lawgiver but Joshua/Jesus leads God's people into the promised rest (Heb 4:8). The crossing of the Jordan is presented by the Catechism, with the crossing of the Red Sea, as a figure of Baptism (CCC 1222). His renewal of the covenant at Shechem (Jos 24) is a model of personal and household fidelity. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on September 1.
know: Renamed from Hoshea by Moses (Num 13:16).
One of only two adults of the Exodus generation to enter Canaan (Num 14:30).
Led the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho (Jos 3-6).
Commanded the sun to stand still at Gibeon (Jos 10:12-14).
'As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (Jos 24:15).

name: Peter
summary: Simon, a Galilean fisherman from Bethsaida living at Capernaum, was brought to Jesus by his brother Andrew and renamed Cephas, 'Rock' (Peter). He confessed Jesus as 'the Christ, the Son of the living God', received the keys of the Kingdom, witnessed the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane, and denied Jesus three times during the Passion. The risen Lord appeared to him and three times charged him to feed his sheep; in Acts he leads the Church, preaching at Pentecost and receiving the first Gentiles.
catholic: Jesus' words 'You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church ... I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven' (Mt 16:18-19) ground the Petrine office: Peter is to strengthen his brethren (Lk 22:32) and feed Christ's flock (Jn 21:15-17), a ministry continued by his successors, the Bishops of Rome (CCC 552-553, 881). The Church is built on the faith he confessed (CCC 424). Tradition holds he was crucified head downward in Rome under Nero, and St Peter's Basilica stands over his tomb. His triple denial and triple profession of love make him a model of repentance and mercy.
know: Son of John/Jonah and brother of Andrew (Jn 1:40-42; Mt 16:17).
Married: Jesus healed his mother-in-law (Mk 1:29-31).
Always named first in the lists of the Twelve (Mt 10:2).
Traditionally the author of 1 and 2 Peter; Mark's Gospel is said to preserve his preaching.
Feasts June 29 (Sts Peter and Paul) and February 22 (Chair of St Peter).
feast: June 29 (Sts Peter and Paul); February 22 (Chair of St Peter)

name: Paul
summary: Saul of Tarsus was a zealous Pharisee, trained under Gamaliel, who approved of Stephen's stoning and persecuted the Church. The risen Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus; he was baptized by Ananias and became the great missionary to the Gentiles. His three missionary journeys (Acts 13-20) planted churches across Asia Minor and Greece, and his letters form the largest part of the New Testament. Arrested in Jerusalem, he appealed to Caesar and was brought as a prisoner to Rome, where Acts leaves him preaching openly.
catholic: The Church honors Paul as 'the Apostle' par excellence, celebrating both his Conversion (January 25) and, together with Peter, the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul (June 29), the twin pillars of the Church of Rome. Tradition holds that he was martyred by beheading at Rome under Nero; his tomb is venerated at the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls. His conversion shows that the risen Christ appeared to him 'last of all, as to one untimely born' (1 Cor 15:8; CCC 659), and that persecuting the Church is persecuting Christ himself ('why are you persecuting me?'), a foundation of the doctrine of the Church as the Body of Christ. His letters supply core Catholic teaching on justification by grace through faith working in love, the Eucharist (1 Cor 11:23-29), the Church as Body and Bride of Christ (Eph 5), and the laying on of hands for ordination (2 Tim 1:6; CCC 1590). At the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15) he submitted the circumcision question to the apostles and elders, and he went up to Jerusalem to confer with Peter (Gal 1:18), a model of communion with apostolic authority.
know: Born a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin in Tarsus and a Roman citizen by birth (Acts 22:3, 22:28; Phil 3:5).
Converted on the road to Damascus (Acts 9, retold in Acts 22 and 26); feast of his Conversion January 25.
Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name (Romans through Philemon).
Acts uses 'Saul' until Acts 13:9 ('Saul, who is also called Paul') and 'Paul' thereafter.
A nephew, his sister's son, warned him of a plot against his life (Acts 23:16).

name: Joseph
role: Son of Jacob; ruler of Egypt
summary: Rachel's firstborn and Jacob's favourite, given a special coat and dreams of his family bowing to him. His jealous brothers sold him to traders, and in Egypt he served Potiphar, was falsely accused by Potiphar's wife and imprisoned, and interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's officials and of Pharaoh himself. Made governor of Egypt, he stored grain against famine, tested and then forgave his brothers, and brought Jacob's whole family to Egypt; he died at 110 asking that his bones be carried to Canaan.
catholic: The Fathers saw Joseph as one of the clearest types of Christ: the beloved son, rejected and sold by his brothers for silver, humiliated and then exalted, who forgives those who wronged him and saves them from death. The Catechism quotes his words to his brothers, 'It was not you who sent me here, but God... you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good', to show how God's providence draws good even from evil (CCC 312; Gen 45:8; 50:20). Pharaoh's command 'Go to Joseph' (Gen 41:55) was applied to St Joseph, and Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Quamquam pluries (1889) compares the patriarch, guardian of Egypt's grain, with the guardian of the Holy Family. Sirach praises him: 'nor was there a man born like Joseph' (Sir 49:15).
know: Favourite son of Jacob; the coat and the dreams (Gen 37)
Sold by his brothers for twenty pieces of silver (Gen 37:28)
Resisted Potiphar's wife; imprisoned (Gen 39)
Interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and became governor of Egypt (Gen 41)
Forgave his brothers: 'God meant it for good' (Gen 50:20)

name: Judas Maccabeus
summary: The third son of Mattathias, surnamed Maccabaeus ('the hammer'), who led the revolt after his father's death. With small forces he defeated Apollonius, Seron, Gorgias, Nicanor and Lysias, purified and rededicated the Temple on 25 Chislev 164 BC — the origin of Hanukkah — and made an alliance with Rome. He was killed fighting Bacchides at Elasa (160 BC).
catholic: 1 and 2 Maccabees are deuterocanonical books, received in the Church's canon (Rome 382, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Florence, and defined at Trent in 1546) though not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament. Judas is central to the Church's doctrine of prayer for the dead: after a battle he took up a collection and sent it to Jerusalem for a sin offering for fallen soldiers, 'for if he wasn't expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would be superfluous and idle to pray for the dead' (2 Macc 12:43-45). The Catechism cites this passage in its teaching on purgatory and the Church's practice of offering suffrages, especially the Eucharistic sacrifice, for the dead (CCC 1032; the verse is numbered 12:46 in the Vulgate). Jesus himself kept the feast Judas instituted, the Feast of the Dedication (John 10:22).
know: Surnamed Maccabaeus, 'the hammer' (1 Macc 2:4).
Rededicated the Temple, origin of Hanukkah (1 Macc 4:36-59).
Prayer and sacrifice for the dead (2 Macc 12:38-45).
Vision of Onias and Jeremiah giving him a golden sword (2 Macc 15:12-16).
Killed at Elasa and buried at Modin (1 Macc 9:5-19).

name: Jeremiah
summary: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, of a priestly family of Anathoth, was called as a youth in the 13th year of Josiah and prophesied for some forty years until after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. He warned Judah to repent and later to submit to Babylon, enduring beatings, the stocks, prison and a muddy cistern; his scribe Baruch wrote down his oracles. After Gedaliah's murder he was taken against his will to Egypt.
catholic: The Church sees in Jeremiah, the rejected and suffering prophet who is 'like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter' (Jer 11:19), a striking figure of Christ in his Passion; some even took Jesus for Jeremiah (Mt 16:14). His promise of a New Covenant written on the heart (Jer 31:31-34) is fulfilled in the covenant Christ seals in his Blood at the Last Supper (Lk 22:20; Heb 8:8-12; cf. CCC 64). Matthew sees Rachel weeping (Jer 31:15) fulfilled in the Holy Innocents. 2 Maccabees 15:14 shows Jeremiah in glory as 'he who prays much for the people', a text cited in support of the intercession of the saints.
know: Called before birth: 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you' (Jer 1:5).
Acted out signs: the linen waistband, the potter's house, the broken jar, the yoke.
Thrown into a cistern and rescued by Ebed-melech the Ethiopian (Jer 38).
Promised the New Covenant (Jer 31:31-34) and bought a field at Anathoth as a sign of hope (Jer 32).
Traditionally credited with Lamentations; Tradition holds he died in Egypt.

name: Isaac
summary: The son of the promise, born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age and named 'laughter'. As a youth he was bound on the altar on Mount Moriah until God provided a ram. He married Rebekah, who bore the twins Esau and Jacob; in old age and blind, he was deceived into giving Jacob the blessing meant for Esau. He died at 180 and was buried by his sons.
catholic: The Church sees in the binding of Isaac (the Akedah) a figure of Christ's sacrifice: the beloved only son carries the wood up the mountain, is offered by his father, and is received back 'figuratively' from the dead (Heb 11:17-19); Fathers such as Origen compare Isaac carrying the wood to Christ carrying his Cross. The Catechism links Abraham's offering to the Father who 'did not spare his own Son' (CCC 2572). St Paul calls Christians 'children of promise, as Isaac was' (Gal 4:28). God is named 'the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' (Ex 3:6), and Jesus uses this title to teach the resurrection (Mt 22:32).
know: Name means 'he laughs' (Gen 21:3-6)
Bound on Mount Moriah; God provided a ram (Gen 22)
Married Rebekah and loved her (Gen 24:67)
Father of the twins Esau and Jacob (Gen 25:24-26)
Blessed Jacob in place of Esau (Gen 27)

name: Samuel
summary: Samuel, son of Elkanah and Hannah, was given to the LORD as a child and grew up at Shiloh under Eli, where God called him by name in the night. He became prophet, priest-like intercessor and the last judge of Israel, leading the people back to God at Mizpah. At the people's demand he anointed Saul as first king, later rebuked Saul's disobedience, and secretly anointed the boy David at Bethlehem.
catholic: Samuel's night-time call ('Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening') is the Church's favourite text on vocation and listening prayer; the Catechism says he learned to pray from Hannah and Eli (CCC 2578). Scripture ranks him with Moses as a great intercessor (Ps 99:6; Jer 15:1), and Peter calls him the first of the prophets who foretold Christ's days (Acts 3:24). By anointing David he stands at the head of the line of the Anointed (Messiah/Christ) king (CCC 436). The Roman Martyrology commemorates the holy prophet Samuel on August 20.
know: Called by God as a boy in the temple at Shiloh
Last of the judges; a prophet from Dan to Beersheba
Anointed both Saul and David
His sons' corruption led Israel to ask for a king
Summoned from the dead by the medium of Endor

name: Joab
summary: Joab son of Zeruiah, David's nephew, led the capture of Jerusalem and commanded David's army for decades. Loyal but ruthless, he murdered Abner and Amasa, arranged Uriah's death at David's command, engineered Absalom's return and then killed him against orders. He backed Adonijah, and Solomon had him executed at the altar.
know: Captured Jerusalem's stronghold
Killed Abner and Amasa
Carried out David's order to place Uriah in the front line
Killed Absalom
Executed by Benaiah at Solomon's command

name: Hezekiah
summary: Hezekiah son of Ahaz reigned twenty-nine years and trusted the LORD like no king before or after. He reopened and purified the Temple, held a great Passover inviting even the north, and destroyed the high places and Moses' bronze serpent Nehushtan, which had become an idol. When Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem he spread the Assyrian letter before the LORD and, encouraged by Isaiah, saw the city delivered. Healed from mortal illness with the sign of the retreating shadow, he then showed his treasures to Babylonian envoys, and Isaiah foretold exile to Babylon.
catholic: Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's support during Sennacherib's siege are classic examples of trust in God; his canticle of thanksgiving after his healing (Isa 38:10-20) is prayed in the Liturgy of the Hours. Sirach praises him with David and Josiah as the only faithful kings (Sir 49:4), and he is in Jesus' genealogy (Mt 1:9-10). Proverbs 25:1 credits 'the men of Hezekiah' with collecting proverbs of Solomon.
know: Restored the Temple and the Passover
Destroyed the bronze serpent Nehushtan
Prayed when Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem
Healed with 15 more years of life
Built the Siloam water tunnel

name: Nebuchadnezzar
summary: Nebuchadnezzar (II) king of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish, made Jehoiakim his vassal, deported Jehoiachin and the elite of Jerusalem in 597 BC, installed Zedekiah, and after Zedekiah's revolt destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple in 587/586 BC, carrying the people into exile. In Daniel he dreams of the great statue, throws the three young men into the furnace, is humbled by madness and finally praises the Most High.
catholic: Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God's 'servant' (Jer 25:9) - an instrument of judgement who does not know he serves God's purpose. In Daniel 4 his humiliation and restoration show God's sovereignty over the proud kingdoms of the world, and the stone 'cut without hands' that shatters his dream-statue (Dan 2:34-35, 44) is read by the Fathers as Christ and his everlasting Kingdom, the stone born of the Virgin without human father. The Nebuchadnezzar of the Book of Judith, 'king of the Assyrians', is generally read as a literary figure of the arrogant world-power.
know: Destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple (587/586 BC)
Deported Jehoiachin, Daniel and Ezekiel's generation
Dreamed of the statue and the stone (Dan 2)
Cast the three young men into the furnace (Dan 3)
Humbled and restored (Dan 4)

name: Daniel
summary: Daniel, a young noble of Judah taken to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar and renamed Belteshazzar, refused the king's food, interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dreams and the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and was delivered from the lions' den under Darius the Mede. He received visions of four beasts, the Son of Man, seventy weeks and the resurrection; in the Greek chapters he vindicates Susanna and exposes the idol Bel and the dragon.
catholic: The Church reads Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom (Dan 7:13-14) as fulfilled in Christ, who took 'Son of Man' as his own title and quoted this text before the high priest (Mt 26:64). Dan 12:2 is one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to the resurrection of the dead. Daniel's fidelity in prayer and fasting and his deliverance from the lions were favourite images in early Christian art of the saving power of God. The Catholic Bible includes the Greek additions (Dan 3:24-90; 13; 14), and the Roman Martyrology commemorates the holy prophet Daniel on July 21.
know: Renamed Belteshazzar in Babylon (Dan 1:7).
Interpreted the statue dream and the writing on the wall (Dan 2; 5).
Prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem and was saved from the lions (Dan 6; 14).
Saw the Son of Man vision (Dan 7) and was visited by the angel Gabriel (Dan 8-9).
Rescued Susanna by cross-examining the two elders separately (Dan 13).

name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
summary: The king of Egypt whom Moses and Aaron confronted with the LORD's command, 'Let my people go.' He hardened his heart through ten plagues, released Israel only after the death of the firstborn, then pursued them and lost his army in the Red Sea.
catholic: Pharaoh is Scripture's great image of the heart that hardens itself against God; St. Paul cites him in Romans 9:17 on God's sovereignty in salvation history. The deliverance from his power through the sea is, for the Church, the type of Baptism (CCC 1221), and the Easter Vigil's reading of Exodus 14 celebrates Christ's victory over sin and death as the true Exodus.
know: Unnamed in Scripture.
Answered Moses, 'Who is the LORD, that I should listen to his voice?' (Exo 5:2).
Ten plagues culminated in the death of the firstborn (Exo 12:29-32).
His chariots were drowned in the Red Sea (Exo 14:23-28).

name: Elijah
summary: Elijah the Tishbite of Gilead burst onto the scene announcing a drought to Ahab. Fed by ravens at the brook Cherith and by the widow of Zarephath, whose son he raised, he confronted the 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, where fire fell from heaven on his sacrifice. Fleeing Jezebel, he was fed by an angel and walked forty days to Horeb, where God came not in wind, earthquake or fire but in 'a still small voice'. He called Elisha, condemned Ahab over Naboth, and was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind with a chariot of fire.
catholic: Elijah is the 'father' of the prophets; the Catechism presents his prayer and Carmel sacrifice as a model of prayer and conversion (CCC 2582-2583), and his fire from heaven as a figure of the fire of the Holy Spirit (CCC 696). Malachi foretold his return before the day of the LORD, and Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come (Mt 11:14; 17:10-13; cf. Lk 1:17; CCC 718). At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, speak with Jesus of his exodus (CCC 555). The angel's bread that strengthened him for forty days is read with the Bread of Life discourse (19th Sunday, Year B) as a figure of the Eucharist, and his forty-day journey shapes Lent. The Carmelite Order venerates him as its spiritual father and model of contemplation; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on July 20, which Carmelites keep as his feast.

name: Absalom
summary: Absalom, David's handsome third son by Maacah, avenged his sister Tamar by killing Amnon and fled to Geshur. Restored through Joab, he won the hearts of Israel and raised a revolt at Hebron, driving David from Jerusalem and taking his concubines. Defeated in the forest of Ephraim, he was caught by his hair in an oak and killed by Joab, and David wept, 'O my son Absalom!'
catholic: David's grief over Absalom - 'would that I had died instead of you' - is often read as an image of the Father's love for rebellious children. The Mount of Olives ascent of the weeping, barefoot David betrayed by his son and his counsellor Ahithophel (2 Sam 15:30-31) is read by the Fathers as a figure of Christ's agony and betrayal on the same mount.

name: Esau
role: Elder son of Isaac; ancestor of Edom
summary: The elder twin of Isaac and Rebekah, a red and hairy hunter loved by Isaac. He sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal of lentil stew and later lost his father's blessing to Jacob's deception, vowing to kill him. Twenty years later he ran to meet Jacob and embraced him, and he settled in Seir; he is the father of the Edomites.
catholic: Hebrews warns against being 'profane like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal' (Heb 12:16-17), and St Paul cites 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' (Rom 9:13; Mal 1:2-3) to show the freedom of God's election, a Semitic idiom of preference rather than a statement of personal damnation. His generous reconciliation with Jacob (Gen 33) is a striking picture of forgiveness.

name: Jonathan Maccabeus
summary: The youngest son of Mattathias, surnamed Apphus, who succeeded Judas as leader (160 BC). Skilfully playing rival Seleucid claimants against each other, he was named high priest by Alexander Balas (152 BC), renewed alliances with Rome and Sparta, and extended Jewish control, until the general Tryphon lured him into Ptolemais, captured him by treachery and later killed him.
catholic: 1 and 2 Maccabees are deuterocanonical books, received in the Church's canon (Rome 382, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Florence, and defined at Trent in 1546) though not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament. Jonathan's investiture as high priest at the Feast of Tabernacles (1 Macc 10:21) began the Hasmonean high priesthood outside the line of Zadok, a turning point in the history of the priesthood that forms the background of the Gospels.

name: Jonathan
summary: Jonathan, Saul's eldest son, was a brave warrior who with only his armour-bearer routed a Philistine garrison at Michmash. He loved David 'as his own soul', made a covenant with him, gave him his robe and weapons, and warned him of Saul's plots, accepting that David, not he, would be king. He died beside his father on Mount Gilboa, and David lamented him and later cared for his son Mephibosheth.
catholic: The friendship of David and Jonathan is the Bible's great portrait of covenant friendship: self-giving, faithful and rooted in God. Jonathan's yielding of his own claim to the throne to God's chosen one is often compared with John the Baptist's 'He must increase, I must decrease'. David's lament (2 Sam 1:17-27) is one of the most moving elegies in Scripture.

name: Ahab
summary: Ahab son of Omri reigned twenty-two years in Samaria and 'did more to provoke the LORD' than all the kings before him. He married Jezebel of Sidon, built a temple and altar to Baal, and clashed repeatedly with the prophet Elijah - over the drought, on Mount Carmel, and after Jezebel had Naboth murdered for his vineyard. He won victories over Ben-hadad but spared him, ignored Micaiah's warning, and died at Ramoth-gilead from a random arrow, the dogs licking his blood as Elijah had foretold.
catholic: Ahab is Scripture's image of the weak ruler led by a wicked spouse into idolatry and injustice; Naboth's vineyard, retold by St. Ambrose in 'On Naboth', became a classic text on the sin of greed and abuse of the poor. Yet when Ahab humbled himself at Elijah's word, God delayed the disaster (1 Kgs 21:27-29) - a sign of God's readiness to show mercy even to great sinners.

name: John the Baptist
summary: Son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, John lived in the wilderness, wore camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey. He preached a baptism of repentance in the Jordan, baptized Jesus, and pointed him out as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world'. Imprisoned by Herod Antipas for condemning his marriage to Herodias, he was beheaded at the request of Herodias's daughter.
catholic: John is the Lord's immediate precursor, 'more than a prophet', the last of the prophets of the Old Covenant and the voice foretold by Isaiah (CCC 523, 717-720). Jesus identifies him with the Elijah who was to come (Mt 11:14). His words 'Behold the Lamb of God' are repeated at every Mass before Communion. Besides Christ and Mary he is the only saint whose birth is celebrated in the calendar (June 24), and his martyrdom is kept on August 29. He is honoured as a martyr for truth and for the sanctity of marriage.

name: Jeroboam I
summary: Jeroboam son of Nebat, an able Ephraimite overseer under Solomon, was told by the prophet Ahijah, who tore his new cloak into twelve pieces, that he would rule ten tribes. He fled to Shishak in Egypt, returned after Solomon's death and became first king of the northern kingdom. To keep the people from going to Jerusalem he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan with non-Levitical priests and his own feast - 'the sin of Jeroboam' by which every later northern king is judged.
catholic: Jeroboam's calves - a political religion cut off from the Temple and the lawful priesthood - became the paradigm of schism in Scripture. Catholic commentators have long drawn from his story the lesson that unity of worship and lawful priesthood belong to God's covenant, a theme fulfilled in Christ's prayer 'that they may all be one' (Jn 17:21).

name: Jehoshaphat
summary: Jehoshaphat son of Asa reigned twenty-five years and walked in the LORD's ways: he sent Levites to teach the law in the cities and appointed judges, charging them to judge in the fear of the LORD. He allied with Ahab by marriage and fought beside him at Ramoth-gilead, where Micaiah prophesied. Facing a great Moabite-Ammonite invasion he proclaimed a fast and sent singers ahead of the army, and God gave the victory.
catholic: Jehoshaphat's prayer 'we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you' (2 Chr 20:12) and the victory won through praise are classic texts on trust and liturgical prayer. He is an ancestor of Jesus (Mt 1:8). His alliance with Ahab's house, sealed by marrying his son to Athaliah, nearly destroyed David's line.

name: Pharaoh (in Joseph's time)
summary: The unnamed king of Egypt whose dreams of seven fat and seven lean cows Joseph interpreted. He made Joseph ruler over all Egypt, renamed him Zaphenath-Paneah, gave him Asenath as wife, and welcomed Jacob's family to settle in Goshen.
catholic: His command to the starving people, 'Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do' (Gen 41:55), was taken up in devotion to St Joseph ('Ite ad Ioseph'), and readers have noted its echo in Mary's words at Cana, 'Whatever he says to you, do it' (Jn 2:5).

name: Simon Maccabeus
summary: The second son of Mattathias, surnamed Thassi, called by his father 'a man of counsel'. After Jonathan's murder he led the nation, won full independence in 142 BC ('the yoke of the Gentiles was taken away from Israel'), took the citadel of Jerusalem, and was confirmed by the people as leader and high priest 'forever, until there should arise a faithful prophet'. He was murdered with two sons by his son-in-law Ptolemy at Dok near Jericho (134 BC).
catholic: 1 and 2 Maccabees are deuterocanonical books, received in the Church's canon (Rome 382, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Florence, and defined at Trent in 1546) though not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament. The hymn on Simon's reign (1 Macc 14:4-15) — every man under his vine and fig tree, peace in the land — uses messianic language from the prophets (Mic 4:4; Zech 3:10), while the people's decree that his rule last 'until a faithful prophet should arise' (1 Macc 14:41) shows Israel still awaiting the definitive prophet whom the New Testament proclaims in Christ.

name: Eleazar
summary: Third son of Aaron, who succeeded his father as high priest when Moses transferred Aaron's vestments to him on Mount Hor. He took the census on the plains of Moab, commissioned Joshua with Moses, and with Joshua divided the land among the tribes; he was buried in the hill country of Ephraim.
catholic: Eleazar embodies the continuity of the priesthood through succession: the office passes from Aaron to his son by a visible rite of investiture. The Church sees in this an Old Testament witness to an ordered, handed-on priesthood, fulfilled in Christ and continued in the ministerial priesthood.

Father of Phinehas.

name: Balaam
summary: Diviner from Pethor by the Euphrates, son of Beor, hired by King Balak of Moab to curse Israel. God stopped him through a talking donkey and an angel, and instead of cursing he blessed Israel four times, prophesying 'a star will come out of Jacob, a scepter will rise out of Israel.' He later counselled Moab and Midian to lead Israel into sin at Peor and was killed with the kings of Midian.
catholic: Balaam's oracle of the star out of Jacob (Num 24:17) was read by Origen and other Fathers as fulfilled in the star that led the Magi to Christ. The New Testament treats Balaam as a type of the false teacher who sells his gift for gain (2 Pet 2:15; Jude 11; Rev 2:14), a warning the Church applies to anyone who traffics in sacred things.

Blessed Israel instead of cursing (Num 23-24).
Prophesied 'a star will come out of Jacob' (Num 24:17).

name: Zedekiah
summary: Zedekiah (Mattaniah), son of Josiah and uncle of Jehoiachin, was installed by Nebuchadnezzar and renamed. Weak and vacillating, he consulted Jeremiah secretly yet let him be imprisoned, and finally rebelled against Babylon. After an eighteen-month siege Jerusalem fell in 587/586 BC; Zedekiah fled, was captured near Jericho, saw his sons killed at Riblah, was blinded and taken to Babylon in chains.
catholic: Zedekiah is the tragic end of the earthly Davidic kingship - a king who knew God's word through Jeremiah but lacked courage to obey it. The end of the monarchy turns Israel's hope toward the promised righteous Branch of David (Jer 23:5-6; 33:15), fulfilled in Christ (2 Chr 36 is read on the 4th Sunday of Lent, Year B).

name: Elisha
summary: Elisha son of Shaphat was ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah cast his mantle on him; he slaughtered the oxen, fed the people and followed. He asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, saw him taken up, and parted the Jordan with his mantle. For some fifty years he worked many miracles - purifying Jericho's spring, multiplying a widow's oil, raising the Shunammite's son, feeding a hundred men with twenty loaves, healing Naaman, making an axe-head float - advised kings, anointed Jehu through a disciple, and foretold Hazael's rule. Even after death a corpse touching his bones came to life.
catholic: Elisha's miracles foreshadow Christ's: the feeding of a hundred with twenty barley loaves 'and some was left over' (2 Kgs 4:42-44) is read with Jesus' feeding of the five thousand (17th Sunday, Year B); the raising of the Shunammite's son near Shunem anticipates Jesus raising the widow's son at nearby Nain (Lk 7:11-17); and the cleansing of Naaman in the Jordan prefigures Baptism (Lk 4:27). His call - leaving everything to follow Elijah - is read with Jesus' demands on would-be disciples (13th Sunday, Year C). The dead man revived by touching his bones (2 Kgs 13:21) has long been cited in support of the veneration of relics. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on June 14.

name: Isaiah
summary: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (8th century BC). Called in a vision of the thrice-holy Lord in the Temple, he urged King Ahaz to trust God rather than Assyria, gave him the sign of the virgin who would bear a son named Immanuel, and later strengthened Hezekiah during Sennacherib's siege and his illness. The book bearing his name also contains the Servant Songs and the great oracles of comfort and of the new Jerusalem.
catholic: The Church reads Isaiah more than any other prophet in the liturgy, especially in Advent and Christmas; St Jerome called him an evangelist rather than a prophet. Isa 7:14 is read as the prophecy of the virginal conception of Christ (Mt 1:23; CCC 497), Isa 9 and 11 as the birth and Spirit-anointing of the Messiah (Isa 11:1-2 is the scriptural root of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, CCC 712, 1831), and the Suffering Servant of Isa 52:13-53:12 as Christ in his Passion (CCC 601, 713). The seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' (Isa 6:3) is sung in the Sanctus of every Mass, and Jesus opened his ministry by reading Isa 61:1-2 in Nazareth. Isaiah 54 and 55 are read at the Easter Vigil.
know: Son of Amoz; called in a Temple vision of the seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy' (Isa 6).
Gave Ahaz the Immanuel sign: 'the virgin will conceive and bear a son' (Isa 7:14).
His sons' names were living prophecies: Shear-jashub ('a remnant will return') and Maher-shalal-hash-baz.
Counselled Hezekiah during the Assyrian siege and in his sickness (2 Kings 19-20).

name: Pontius Pilate
summary: Pontius Pilate was Roman prefect of Judea (AD 26-36). At the Passion he questioned Jesus about his kingship ('What is truth?'), found no basis for a charge, sent him to Herod, offered to release him, then had him scourged, presented him to the crowd, released Barabbas, washed his hands, and handed Jesus over to be crucified, posting the inscription 'King of the Jews'.
catholic: Pilate is named in the Creed - 'suffered under Pontius Pilate' - which anchors the Passion in real, datable history. The Church sees in him the weakness of a judge who knew the truth but yielded to fear and expediency. His existence is confirmed by Roman historians and by the 'Pilate stone' found at Caesarea in 1961.

'What is truth?' (Jn 18:38).

name: Abner
summary: Abner son of Ner, Saul's kinsman (his cousin according to 1 Sam 14:50-51), commanded Saul's army and after Saul's death made Ishbosheth king over Israel. He killed Asahel in battle, then quarrelled with Ishbosheth and went over to David, but Joab murdered him at Hebron in revenge; David mourned him publicly.

name: Asa
summary: Asa son of Abijah reigned forty-one years and 'did what was right'. He removed idols and male cult prostitutes, deposed the queen mother Maacah for her Asherah image, and defeated Zerah the Ethiopian by relying on the LORD. Later he bribed Ben-hadad of Damascus against Baasha, imprisoned the seer Hanani who rebuked him, and in his foot disease sought physicians rather than the LORD.

name: Job
summary: A blameless and upright man of the land of Uz, the greatest of the people of the east. With God's permission Satan stripped him of his possessions, his ten children and his health. Job refused to curse God, but in long poetic dialogues with his three friends he protested his innocence and demanded an answer. God spoke from the whirlwind, Job repented in dust and ashes, interceded for his friends and was restored twofold.
catholic: The Church reads Job as the great biblical meditation on innocent suffering. St John Paul II's Salvifici Doloris (1984) uses Job to show that suffering is not always punishment for sin, and that its full meaning is revealed only in the Cross of Christ. The Fathers, especially St Gregory the Great in his Moralia on Job, saw him as a figure of the suffering Christ and of the Church. His cry 'I know that my Redeemer lives' (Job 19:25) is one of the readings offered for funeral Masses, and the traditional Office of the Dead takes its readings from Job. James 5:11 holds up 'the perseverance of Job', and Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel as a model of righteousness. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on May 10.

name: Josiah
summary: Josiah son of Amon became king at eight and reigned thirty-one years, the great reforming king. While the Temple was being repaired the high priest Hilkiah found the book of the law; Josiah tore his clothes, consulted the prophetess Huldah, read the covenant to the people and renewed it, purged idolatry from Jerusalem to Bethel (fulfilling a prophecy made three centuries earlier) and celebrated an unequalled Passover. He was killed at Megiddo opposing Pharaoh Necoh, and Jeremiah lamented him.
catholic: Josiah is praised as having no equal in turning to the LORD 'with all his heart, soul and might' (2 Kgs 23:25) - the words of the Shema - and Sirach says his memory is 'like incense' (Sir 49:1). His reform shows renewal flowing from the rediscovered Word of God and the liturgy (Passover). He stands in Jesus' genealogy (Mt 1:10-11), and the mourning for him at Megiddo is recalled in Zechariah 12:11, a text John applies to the Pierced One.

name: Gideon
summary: Son of Joash of the clan of Abiezer in Manasseh, called by the angel of the LORD while threshing wheat in a winepress during the Midianite oppression. He tore down his father's altar of Baal (earning the name Jerubbaal), sought signs with a fleece, and with only three hundred men bearing trumpets and torches in jars routed the Midianite host. He refused kingship, but his gold ephod became a snare to Israel.
catholic: The Fathers, notably St. Ambrose, read the fleece wet with dew while the ground stayed dry as a figure of the Virgin Mary, who received the Word as dew from heaven; the Liturgy of the Hours for January 1 sings that Christ came down 'like rain upon the fleece'. Gideon's small band shows that victory comes from God, not from human strength. Hebrews 11:32 names him among the heroes of faith, and the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on September 1.

name: Mordecai
role: Jewish official at the Persian court
summary: A Benjamite exile at Susa who raised his orphaned cousin Esther. He uncovered a plot against King Ahasuerus, refused to bow to Haman, and when Haman decreed the destruction of the Jews, urged Esther to intercede. Haman's plot recoiled on himself; Mordecai was honored, became the king's chief minister and, with Esther, established Purim. His prophetic dream frames the Greek book.
catholic: The Catholic canon reads Esther in its longer Greek form: the six 'additions' (Mordecai's dream, the royal letters, the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, Esther's approach to the king and the dream's interpretation) are deuterocanonical and canonical Scripture, defined at Trent; in this text they appear in square brackets within chapters 1-10. In his prayer (Est 4:18-28) Mordecai explains that he refused to bow to Haman not from pride but 'that I might not set the glory of man above the glory of God' — a witness to the first commandment. His dream and its fulfilment (Est 1:1; 10:4-13) show that God governs history even where his name is hidden. 2 Maccabees calls the eve of Purim 'Mordecai's day' (2 Macc 15:36).

He made Jacob serve seven years for Rachel, then substituted Leah on the wedding night, and changed Jacob's wages ten times. When Jacob fled with his daughters, Laban pursued him, and they made a covenant at the heap of Galeed.
catholic: Laban is remembered as a figure of craftiness overruled by God's providence; Judith recalls how God tested Jacob 'when he kept the sheep of Laban' (Jdt 8:26).

name: Noah
summary: A righteous man, blameless in his generation, who 'walked with God'. When God resolved to send the Flood on a corrupt earth, he commanded Noah to build an ark and bring his family and the animals into it. After the waters receded, Noah built an altar, and God made a covenant with him and all living creatures, sealed by the rainbow. He planted a vineyard, became drunk, and cursed Canaan after Ham's disrespect; he lived 950 years.
catholic: The Catechism teaches that the covenant with Noah, God's covenant with all nations, 'remains in force during the times of the Gentiles' (CCC 56-58, 71), and counts Noah among the righteous of the nations (CCC 58). The ark is a classic figure of the Church, 'which alone saves from the flood' (CCC 845), and the Flood waters prefigure Baptism (CCC 1219; 1 Pt 3:20-21), as the Easter Vigil blessing of water recalls. His upright offering after the Flood is cited in the Catechism's history of prayer (CCC 2569). Jesus compares the days of Noah with the coming of the Son of Man (Mt 24:37-39).

name: Sarah
summary: Wife and half-sister of Abraham, long barren. She gave her servant Hagar to Abraham, then resented her. God renamed her from Sarai to Sarah and promised her a son; she laughed at the promise but bore Isaac at ninety. She died at 127 in Hebron and was buried in the cave of Machpelah.
catholic: Hebrews praises Sarah's faith in receiving power to conceive (Heb 11:11), and 1 Peter holds her up as a model for Christian wives (1 Pt 3:6). St Paul makes her, the free woman, an image of the 'Jerusalem above' who is mother of believers (Gal 4:22-31). Her miraculous motherhood is among the Old Testament signs preparing for Mary's virginal motherhood (CCC 489). The traditional Roman nuptial blessing prayed that the bride be 'long-lived and faithful like Sarah'.

name: Jehu
summary: Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi, an army commander famous for driving 'furiously', was anointed king by a disciple of Elisha, as God had told Elijah at Horeb. He killed Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, had Jezebel thrown down, wiped out Ahab's house, and slaughtered the worshippers of Baal in their temple. Yet he kept Jeroboam's calves; God promised his sons the throne to the fourth generation.
catholic: Jehu carries out God's judgement on Ahab's house as Elijah foretold, but Hosea condemns 'the blood of Jezreel' (Hos 1:4) - zeal for God's cause cannot excuse cruelty or a divided heart. The Fathers use him as an example of zeal that stops halfway.
know: Anointed at Ramoth-gilead by Elisha's disciple
Drove 'furiously'
Killed Joram, Ahaziah and Jezebel
Destroyed Baal worship in Israel
His dynasty lasted four more generations

name: Haman
summary: Son of Hammedatha (called 'the Bugaean', and in the Greek letter 'the Macedonian'), exalted above all the king's princes. Enraged that Mordecai would not bow to him, he cast lots (purim) and obtained a royal decree to destroy all the Jews of the empire, built a gallows for Mordecai, and was instead hanged on it when Esther exposed him.
catholic: Haman embodies pride and hatred of God's people; his fall on his own gallows illustrates the biblical theme that the wicked fall into the pit they dig (Ps 7:15-16). Mordecai's dream presents him and Mordecai as the two warring 'serpents' (Est 10:7).
know: Son of Hammedatha (Est 3:1).
Cast lots (purim) to fix the day of destruction (Est 3:7; 9:24).
Forced to honor Mordecai publicly (Est 6:6-11).
Hanged on the gallows built for Mordecai (Est 7:9-10).

name: Judah
role: Son of Jacob; ancestor of the royal tribe
summary: Fourth son of Jacob and Leah. He proposed selling Joseph rather than killing him; later he fathered Perez and Zerah by his daughter-in-law Tamar, admitting 'She is more righteous than I.' In Egypt he offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, moving Joseph to reveal himself. Jacob blessed him as a lion from whom 'the sceptre will not depart'.
catholic: Jacob's blessing, 'The sceptre will not depart from Judah... until he comes to whom it belongs; to him will the obedience of the peoples be' (Gen 49:10), has been read by Jewish and Christian tradition as messianic, fulfilled in Christ the Son of David. 'It is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah' (Heb 7:14), and Christ is 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah' (Rev 5:5). Judah's transformation, from selling Joseph to offering his life for Benjamin, is a powerful example of repentance and substitution.
know: Fourth son of Jacob and Leah; name linked to 'praise' (Gen 29:35)
Proposed selling Joseph (Gen 37:26-27)
Father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar (Gen 38)
Offered himself in Benjamin's place (Gen 44:18-34)
'The sceptre will not depart from Judah' (Gen 49:10)

name: Jesse
summary: Bethlehemite, son of Obed and grandson of Boaz and Ruth, father of eight sons, the youngest of whom, David, was anointed king by Samuel. His name stands at the close of the book of Ruth as the link to David.
catholic: Isaiah's prophecy of 'a shoot from the stock of Jesse' on whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest (Isa 11:1-2) is read by the Church as fulfilled in Christ, and Paul cites 'the root of Jesse' (Rom 15:12). From this text come the medieval 'Tree of Jesse' images and the Advent Jesse Tree, and the 'O Radix Jesse' antiphon of the O Antiphons (December 19). Tradition has also seen Mary as the 'rod' (virga) from Jesse's root.
know: Son of Obed (Ruth 4:22).
A Bethlehemite with eight sons (1 Sam 16:1; 17:12).
Father of King David.
'A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse' (Isa 11:1).

name: John, son of Zebedee
summary: John, a fisherman and brother of James, left his father Zebedee to follow Jesus and with Peter and James formed the inner circle of the Twelve. He and Peter prepared the Passover and later preached together in Jerusalem and Samaria. Catholic tradition identifies him with 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', who leaned on Jesus' breast at the Last Supper, stood at the cross and received Mary as his mother, and ran to the empty tomb.
catholic: The Church honours John as Apostle and Evangelist, by tradition author of the Fourth Gospel, three letters and the Book of Revelation, whose symbol is the eagle. In receiving Mary at the foot of the cross (Jn 19:26-27) he represents every disciple entrusted to her motherly care (CCC 964). Paul names him a 'pillar' of the Church (Gal 2:9). Tradition holds he was exiled to Patmos and died in old age at Ephesus, the only apostle not martyred.
know: Son of Zebedee; brother of James; called Boanerges (Mk 3:17).
Traditionally 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (Jn 13:23; 19:26).
Took Mary into his home (Jn 19:27).
Traditionally the author of John, 1-3 John and Revelation.
Feast December 27.

name: Rachel
summary: Laban's younger daughter, beautiful and beloved by Jacob, who served fourteen years for her. Long barren, she gave him her servant Bilhah, then bore Joseph. She stole her father's household idols when the family fled. She died giving birth to Benjamin on the road to Ephrath (Bethlehem) and was buried there.
catholic: Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping for her children going into exile (Jer 31:15), and Matthew applies the verse to the massacre of the Holy Innocents at Bethlehem (Mt 2:18), read on their feast (28 December). Her long barrenness and joyful motherhood make her one of the Old Testament mothers whose children came by God's gift. The traditional Roman nuptial blessing prayed that the bride be 'loving to her husband like Rachel'.
know: Jacob served fourteen years for her (Gen 29:18-30)
Mother of Joseph and Benjamin

Died giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem (Gen 35:16-20)

name: Holofernes
summary: Chief general of 'Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians', sent to punish the western nations and destroy all worship but the king's. He besieged Bethulia and cut off its water, but was beguiled by Judith's beauty, drank himself into a stupor at a banquet and was beheaded by her with his own sword.
catholic: The Fathers read Holofernes as an image of the proud power of evil, overthrown by the weakness of a faithful woman (Jdt 9:10-11; 16:5-6) — the pattern of Mary's Magnificat, 'He has put down the mighty from their thrones' (Luke 1:52).
know: Second only to Nebuchadnezzar (Jdt 2:4).
Besieged Bethulia (Jdt 7).
Beheaded by Judith (Jdt 13:6-10).

name: Rehoboam
summary: Rehoboam son of Solomon and Naamah went to Shechem to be made king, but rejected the elders' advice and answered the people harshly - 'my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions' - so the ten northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam. Shemaiah stopped him from waging war on Israel. In his reign Shishak of Egypt plundered Jerusalem; he reigned seventeen years.
catholic: Rehoboam's folly fulfils Ahijah's prophecy and shows how pride divides God's people; the Church has often read the schism of Israel and Judah as a warning against division and a longing for the unity Christ restores (cf. Ezek 37:15-22; Jn 11:52). He is an ancestor of Jesus (Mt 1:7).

name: Asaph
summary: Asaph son of Berechiah, a Levite of the Gershonite line, was appointed by David as chief of the Temple singers with cymbals. Twelve psalms bear his name (Ps 50 and 73-83), and his descendants, 'the sons of Asaph', served as singers down to the return from exile. He is also called 'the seer'.
catholic: The psalms of Asaph, prayed daily in the Liturgy of the Hours, include Psalm 50 on true sacrifice ('offer to God the sacrifice of thanksgiving') and Psalm 73, a meditation on the prosperity of the wicked resolved in the sanctuary. The 'sons of Asaph' singing at the founding of the Second Temple (Ezra 3:10) link him to the restoration. Note: psalm superscriptions are not included in this Bible text's verse data, and Catholic liturgical books often use the Greek/Latin psalm numbering (for most psalms from 10 to 147, one number lower).

Psalms 50 and 73-83 bear his name.

name: Balak
summary: Son of Zippor and king of Moab, who, afraid of Israel camped on the plains of Moab, summoned Balaam to curse them. He led Balaam to three high places, but each time Balaam blessed Israel instead.
catholic: Balak illustrates that no human power can curse those whom God has blessed; Micah 6:5 calls Israel to remember what Balak plotted and what Balaam answered, as part of recalling the 'righteous acts of the LORD'. Revelation 2:14 recalls how Balaam taught Balak to cast a stumbling block before Israel.
know: Son of Zippor, king of Moab (Num 22:4).
Hired Balaam to curse Israel.
Remembered in Jos 24:9, Jdg 11:25, Mic 6:5 and Rev 2:14.

name: Zadok
summary: Zadok son of Ahitub, a priest descended from Eleazar son of Aaron, served alongside Abiathar under David and carried the Ark when David fled Absalom. He stayed loyal when Abiathar backed Adonijah, anointed Solomon king at the Gihon spring, and became sole chief priest; his descendants held the high priesthood until the Exile.
catholic: Zadok's anointing of Solomon ('Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed Solomon king') became part of the coronation rite of Christian kings. Ezekiel singles out 'the sons of Zadok' as the faithful priests of the restored temple (Ezek 44:15), and the Church sees in the faithful priesthood a figure of the priests of the New Covenant serving Christ.

Co-priest with Abiathar under David

name: Nicanor
summary: A Seleucid general who hated Israel. Under Demetrius I he tried to capture Judas by treachery, threatened to burn the Temple, and was defeated and killed at Adasa on 13 Adar (161 BC); his head and arm were displayed at Jerusalem and the day was kept as 'Nicanor's Day', the day before Mordecai's Day.

name: Esther
summary: A Jewish orphan of the tribe of Benjamin raised by her cousin Mordecai, Esther was chosen queen by King Ahasuerus. When Haman obtained a decree to annihilate the Jews, she fasted and prayed, risked death by approaching the king unsummoned, and at her banquets exposed Haman, who was hanged; the Jews were saved, and the feast of Purim was established.
catholic: The Catholic canon reads Esther in its longer Greek form: the six 'additions' (Mordecai's dream, the royal letters, the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, Esther's approach to the king and the dream's interpretation) are deuterocanonical and canonical Scripture, defined at Trent; in this text they appear in square brackets within chapters 1-10. Esther is a classic type of Mary: the queen who intercedes with the king for her condemned people, spared from the king's law of death ('You shall not die', Est 5:1 in the Greek addition; the Vulgate adds 'this law is not made for you but for all', words medieval writers applied to the Immaculate Conception) and who finds favor in the king's sight. Her humble prayer in the Greek Addition C (Est 4:29-47) is read on Thursday of the First Week of Lent. The Catechism names Esther among the holy women who kept alive the hope of Israel's salvation and prepared for Mary (CCC 64, 489).
know: Daughter of Aminadab, Mordecai's uncle (Est 2:7, 2:15) — called Abihail in the Hebrew text.
'Who knows if you have been made queen for this occasion?' — Mordecai's challenge (Est 4:14).
Fasted three days before going to the king (Est 4:16).
Her prayer: 'Help me. I am destitute, and have no helper but you' (Est 4:31).
Mordecai interprets the 'little spring that became a river' as Esther (Est 10:6).

name: Merari
summary: Third son of Levi. His descendants, the Merarites, carried the boards, bars, pillars and sockets of the tabernacle.

Head of the Merarite Levites, who carried the tabernacle's frames (Num 4:29-33)
Third son of Levi.
Father of Mahli and Mushi.
Merarites carried the tabernacle's frame (Num 4:29-33).

name: Samson
summary: Son of Manoah of Dan, a Nazirite from birth whose strength depended on his consecration. He killed a lion barehanded, married a Philistine woman of Timnah, struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone, and carried off the gates of Gaza. Betrayed by Delilah, who had his hair cut, he was blinded and enslaved; in his death he pulled down the temple of Dagon, killing more Philistines than in his life. He judged Israel twenty years.
catholic: Hebrews 11:32 counts Samson among the heroes of faith. Patristic writers saw him as a type of Christ: his birth announced by an angel, his strength from the Spirit, his betrayal for silver, his outstretched arms between the pillars, and a victory won in his death. At the same time he is a warning about squandering a consecration through sensuality, and his Nazirite vow (Num 6) points to a life wholly given to God.
know: Nazirite from the womb (Jdg 13:5).
Killed a lion and posed the riddle of honey (Jdg 14).
Struck a thousand men with a jawbone (Jdg 15:15).
Betrayed by Delilah, blinded at Gaza (Jdg 16:4-21).
Brought down Dagon's temple (Jdg 16:28-30).

name: Abimelech (son of Gideon)
summary: Son of Gideon by his concubine in Shechem. With money from the temple of Baal Berith he hired men, murdered his seventy brothers on one stone, and was made king at Shechem. After three years God sent an evil spirit between him and Shechem; he destroyed the city, but at Thebez a woman dropped an upper millstone on his head and he had his armour-bearer kill him.
catholic: Abimelech is Scripture's portrait of the usurper who grasps at kingship by violence, the bramble of Jotham's fable; his end illustrates that God repays bloodshed (Jdg 9:56-57). He stands in contrast to the servant-kingship of Christ.
know: Son of Gideon's Shechemite concubine (Jdg 8:31).
Killed seventy brothers (Jdg 9:5).
Ruled Shechem three years (Jdg 9:22).
Mortally wounded by a millstone thrown by a woman (Jdg 9:53; 2 Sam 11:21).

name: Ahaz
summary: Ahaz son of Jotham reigned sixteen years and did evil, even making his son pass through the fire. When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel attacked Jerusalem, he refused Isaiah's call to trust God and ask a sign, and instead made himself a vassal of Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, copying a Damascus altar for the Temple and closing the Temple's doors.
catholic: To the faithless Ahaz Isaiah gave the sign: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' (Isa 7:14), which Matthew sees fulfilled in the virginal conception of Jesus (Mt 1:22-23); the Church reads it on the 4th Sunday of Advent (Year A). Ahaz, who would not ask a sign, thus stands at the threshold of the great Marian prophecy.

Received the Immanuel prophecy
Became Assyria's vassal
Copied a pagan altar for the Temple
Father of Hezekiah

name: Jehoiakim
summary: Jehoiakim (Eliakim), son of Josiah, was installed by Pharaoh Necoh and taxed the land to pay him; he then served Nebuchadnezzar and rebelled. He persecuted the prophets, killing Uriah son of Shemaiah, and cut up and burned Jeremiah's scroll in his brazier column by column. He reigned eleven years.
catholic: Jehoiakim burning the scroll of God's word (Jer 36) is the classic image of a heart that refuses God's word - while the word itself, rewritten, endures. Daniel 1:1 dates the first deportation, including Daniel, to his reign. Matthew's genealogy passes over him.
know: Originally named Eliakim
Installed by Pharaoh Necoh
Burned Jeremiah's scroll
Rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar

name: Lot
summary: Son of Haran and nephew of Abraham, who travelled with him to Canaan. When their herds grew too large they parted, and Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan and settled in Sodom. Abraham rescued him from the four kings; later two angels led him out of Sodom before its destruction, and his wife, looking back, became a pillar of salt. His daughters bore Moab and Ben Ammi by him.
catholic: 2 Peter calls him 'righteous Lot', 'oppressed by the lustful life of the wicked', whom God rescued (2 Pt 2:7-8), and Wisdom 10:6 says Wisdom delivered a righteous man fleeing the fire on the five cities. Jesus points to the days of Lot as a warning to be ready for the Son of Man, adding 'Remember Lot's wife' (Lk 17:28-32).
know: Son of Haran, nephew of Abraham (Gen 11:27)
Chose the Jordan plain and lived in Sodom (Gen 13:10-12)
Rescued by Abraham (Gen 14) and by angels (Gen 19)
His wife became a pillar of salt (Gen 19:26)
Father of Moab and Ben Ammi, ancestors of Moab and Ammon

name: Uzziah (Azariah)
summary: Uzziah, also called Azariah, became king at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years. He prospered while he sought God - building towers, organising the army and loving the soil - but in pride he entered the Temple to burn incense, a priestly act; when the priests resisted he was struck with leprosy and lived isolated until death while his son Jotham governed.
catholic: Isaiah's great vision of the thrice-holy God came 'in the year that King Uzziah died' (Isa 6:1); the seraphim's Sanctus is sung at every Mass. Uzziah's leprosy for usurping the priest's office is often cited to show that priesthood is received, not seized (cf. Heb 5:4). He is in Jesus' genealogy (Mt 1:8-9).

Reigned 52 years

Isaiah's call came the year he died

name: Amaziah
summary: Amaziah son of Joash reigned twenty-nine years. He executed his father's assassins but, following the law, spared their children; he defeated Edom in the Valley of Salt but then worshipped Edom's gods. Provoking Jehoash of Israel to battle, he was defeated and Jerusalem's wall broken; he was later murdered at Lachish.

Defeated Edom, then adopted its gods
Defeated by Jehoash of Israel
Killed by conspirators at Lachish

name: Sihon
summary: Amorite king ruling from Heshbon who refused Israel passage through his land and attacked them; Israel defeated him and took his territory east of the Jordan, which Moses gave to Reuben and Gad.
catholic: The victories over Sihon and Og became part of Israel's liturgical memory of God's saving deeds, celebrated in Psalms 135 and 136 ('for his loving kindness endures forever').
know: King of the Amorites at Heshbon (Num 21:26).
Refused Israel passage and was defeated (Num 21:21-25).
Celebrated in Ps 135:11 and 136:19.

name: Joash (Jehoash) of Judah
summary: Joash son of Ahaziah, hidden as a baby from Athaliah, was crowned at seven by Jehoiada and reigned forty years. He repaired the Temple with a collection chest while Jehoiada lived, but afterwards turned to idols, had Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned, paid off Hazael of Syria with the Temple treasures, and was murdered by his servants.

Repaired the Temple
Turned to idols after Jehoiada died
Had the prophet Zechariah stoned
Assassinated by his servants

name: Leah
summary: Laban's elder daughter, with 'weak' or tender eyes, given to Jacob in place of Rachel on the wedding night. Less loved than her sister, she was blessed with children: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and Dinah, and through her servant Zilpah, Gad and Asher. She was buried at Machpelah beside Jacob's fathers.
catholic: Leah, the unloved wife whom God regarded (Gen 29:31), became the mother of Levi, the priestly tribe, and of Judah, the royal tribe from which Christ was born. With Rachel she is invoked in the blessing on Ruth's marriage as one of the two 'who built the house of Israel' (Ru 4:11), words long echoed in Christian marriage blessings.
know: Elder daughter of Laban (Gen 29:16)
Married to Jacob by Laban's trick (Gen 29:23-25)
Mother of six sons and Dinah, including Levi and Judah
Named Judah saying 'I will praise the LORD' (Gen 29:35)
Buried at Machpelah (Gen 49:31)

name: Mary, Mother of Jesus
summary: A virgin of Nazareth betrothed to Joseph, Mary was greeted by the angel Gabriel and conceived Jesus by the Holy Spirit, answering 'let it be done to me according to your word'. She visited her relative Elizabeth and sang the Magnificat, gave birth in Bethlehem, presented Jesus in the Temple and found him there at twelve. She prompted his first sign at Cana, stood by the cross where Jesus entrusted her to the beloved disciple, and prayed with the apostles awaiting the Spirit.
catholic: The Church professes four Marian dogmas: Mary is the Mother of God (Theotokos), defined at the Council of Ephesus in 431 (CCC 495); she is ever-virgin, before, during and after the birth of Christ (CCC 496-507); she was preserved from all stain of original sin from her conception (Immaculate Conception, defined by Pius IX in 1854; CCC 490-492); and she was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory (Assumption, defined by Pius XII in 1950; CCC 966). The Fathers call her the New Eve, whose obedience untied the knot of Eve's disobedience (St Irenaeus, CCC 494), and she is the Ark of the Covenant where the glory of the Lord dwells (CCC 2676) - Luke's Visitation deliberately echoes David bringing up the Ark (2 Sam 6). From the cross Jesus gave her as mother to the beloved disciple (Jn 19:26-27), which the Church reads as her spiritual motherhood of all believers (CCC 964-970). The 'brothers' of Jesus are understood as kinsmen, not further children of Mary (CCC 500).
know: Mother of God (Theotokos): Council of Ephesus, 431.
Immaculate Conception defined 1854 (Pius IX); Assumption defined 1950 (Pius XII).
Perpetual virgin: James and Joses, called Jesus' 'brothers', are sons of 'another Mary' (Mt 27:56; CCC 500).
Her Magnificat (Lk 1:46-55) is sung daily at Vespers; the Hail Mary joins Gabriel's and Elizabeth's greetings.
Tradition (Protoevangelium of James), not Scripture, names her parents Joachim and Anne.
feast: January 1 (Mary, Mother of God); March 25 (Annunciation); May 31 (Visitation); August 15 (Assumption); September 8 (Nativity of Mary); December 8 (Immaculate Conception)

name: Ahaziah of Judah
summary: Ahaziah son of Jehoram and Athaliah reigned one year, following the counsel of his mother and Ahab's house. Visiting the wounded Joram of Israel at Jezreel, he was caught up in Jehu's revolt and killed.

Son of Athaliah
